extracted.intended_audience: general readers of memoirs, historians, and students of late-19th-century politics and personalities
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from an autobiographical memoir (Andrew Carnegie) recounting personal encounters with prominent statesmen and intellectuals (Gladstone, Morley, Spencer, Blaine) and offering occasional political proposals and reflections. The page mixes anecdote, character sketch, and prescriptive remarks about constitutional/political practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional arrangement: one Parliament with local legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Britain should follow the American example: 'America had many legislatures, but only one Congress. Britain should follow her example, one Parliament and local legislatures (not parliaments) for Ireland, Scotland, and Wales.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local legislatures (analogous to U.S. states) would handle local matters while a single national Parliament would be supreme; this mirrors the U.S. federal structure and is offered as a remedy to the Home Rule/Irish question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguard for Irish legislation (three‑month parliamentary review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed procedural safeguard: 'the acts of the local legislature of Ireland should lie for three months' continuous session upon the table of the House of Commons, subject to adverse action of the House, but becoming operative unless disapproved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clause is presented as necessary to reassure those fearful of secession while permitting local legislation to take effect unless the national House disapproves during a defined period.

rubrics_metrics.name: First resort against refusal to send representatives: stop the mails
rubrics_metrics.description: On dealing with a refusal by a region to send representatives: 'Employed all the resources of civilization--first, stopped the mails.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnegie states this as a practical coercive measure (illustrative of a hardline position) in the context of preventing secession or enforcing representation; it is a policy recommendation rather than a legal rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disestablishment of the English Church as inevitable
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie's view: disestablishment is inevitable because 'it was an anomaly'—no other part of the English‑speaking race favors one religion by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offered as a political forecast and normative argument for separation of church and state in Britain, used to justify republican/modernizing reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present statistics and national facts 'in a simple and direct form'
rubrics_metrics.description: A need identified by Gladstone: 'Why does not some writer take up this subject and present the facts in a simple and direct form to the world?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify Carnegie's work on Triumphant Democracy — guidance to writers: gather, examine, and arrange figures carefully and present them clearly and plainly for public understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical/analytical work requires steady, laborious care
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie's account of preparing Triumphant Democracy: 'It required steady, laborious work. Figures had to be examined and arranged... The second serious illness of my life dates from the strain brought upon me by this work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical warning/guidance: compiling and interpreting national statistics demands meticulous attention, significant effort, and may be intellectually and physically taxing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a great statesman (Gladstone) — personal and intellectual traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie's character sketch: Gladstone was 'devout and sincere', possessed a 'wonderful memory' and 'wonderful judgment', was 'interested in more subjects than perhaps any other man', 'indefatigable' in getting to the bottom of things, and capable of deep religious conviction that sustained his public work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit evaluative criteria for public leadership: sincerity, moral/religious conviction, broad curiosity, extraordinary memory and judgment, and relentless intellectual thoroughness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of an exemplary intellectual/philosopher (Herbert Spencer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traits attributed to Spencer: calm, weighing 'carefully every action, every word', 'one of the most conscientious men', not a scoffer in religion but critical of certain theological doctrines, interested in practical/mechanical devices, and cautious about public speaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit standard for intellectual character: conscientiousness, careful moral reflection, breadth of interest, humility about public performance, and preference for reasoned, measured conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of John Morley (deliberate judgment; honest character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Morley described as 'pessimistic' in outlook, 'deliberate' in judgment, 'Honest John'—no prevarication, firm as a rock in questions, yet with a 'big heart' shown on rare occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as an evaluative sketch: steadiness of judgment, honesty, and principled firmness count as virtues in public/intellectual life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public speaking / banquet preparation (avoid excitements; prepare in private)
rubrics_metrics.description: Account of Spencer's anxiety about speaking at Delmonico's: friends 'secrete me in an anteroom until the last moment' to avoid excitements and allow him to deliver a prepared speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance for nervous or inexperienced public speakers: limit pre-speech excitements, rely on preparation, and use strategies to reduce stage‑fright (e.g., brief seclusion, limited interlocutory conversation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use anecdotes and simple stories to engage intellectuals and audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie records that Spencer and others enjoyed simple American stories and anecdotes ('Spencer liked stories and was a good laugher... American stories seemed to please him').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a rhetorical technique: short, vivid anecdotes and plain language can effectively engage listeners and bridge intellectual differences.
